title: Doctor Allwissend
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 98. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 98, a short comic tale about an ordinary man mistaken for a seer. A poor farmer named Krebs (crayfish) buys an ABC-book and a sign and sets himself up as “Doctor Know-all”; called in by a lord to find stolen money, he unwittingly terrifies the four guilty servants simply by counting them aloud as each dish is carried in — “Grethe, that was the first” — and they confess to him one after another, certain he has found them out by magic. His own dismay at a covered dish of crayfish (“Ah, poor Krebs that I am!”) is taken by everyone present as the cleverest guess of all.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein armer Bauer Namens Krebs, der fuhr mit zwei Ochsen ein Fuder Holz in die Stadt und verkaufte es für zwei Thaler an einen Doctor.
sentences.l: There was once a poor farmer by the name of Krebs, who drove a load of wood into the town with two oxen and sold it for two thaler to a doctor.
sentences.i: There was once a poor farmer named Krebs, who drove a load of wood into the town with two oxen and sold it to a doctor for two thalers.
sentences.n: Krebs is the man’s name and at the same time the word for a crab or crayfish; the whole tale turns on that double sense, so the name is left standing. Namens is a bare genitive used adverbially, by name. Ein Fuder is a cart-load, as much as one wagon carries.

sentences.t: Wie ihm nun das Geld ausbezahlt wurde, saß der Doctor gerade zu Tisch:
sentences.l: When now the money was being paid out to him, the doctor was just sitting at table:
sentences.i: As the money was being counted out to him, the doctor was just sitting down to his meal:
sentences.n: wie here means when, not how — you will meet it constantly in these tales. “zu Tisch sitzen” is to be at table, at a meal. ausbezahlen is separable, to pay out.

sentences.t: da sah der Bauer wie er schön aß und trank, und das Herz gieng ihm danach auf und er wäre auch gern ein Doctor gewesen.
sentences.l: then the farmer saw how finely he ate and drank, and the heart went open to him at it, and he too would gladly have been a doctor.
sentences.i: and the farmer saw how well he ate and drank, and his heart opened at the sight of it, and he too would gladly have been a doctor.
sentences.n: “das Herz gieng ihm auf” — the heart opened to him — is the idiom for a sudden longing or delight; the person stands in the dative, ihm, where English uses a possessive. gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: Also blieb er noch ein Weilchen stehen und fragte endlich ob er nicht auch könnte ein Doctor werden.
sentences.l: So he remained standing a little while longer and asked at last whether he could not become a doctor too.
sentences.i: So he stayed standing a little while longer, and asked at last whether he too might not become a doctor.
sentences.n: also here is “so, accordingly,” not “also.” “stehen bleiben” is to remain standing, that is, to stop. ein Weilchen is the diminutive of Weile, a little while.

sentences.t: „O ja,“ sagte der Doctor, „das ist bald geschehen.“
sentences.l: “Oh yes,” said the doctor, “that is soon done.”
sentences.n: “das ist bald geschehen” — that is soon happened — is the everyday way of saying a thing is quickly managed.

sentences.t: „Was muß ich thun?“ fragte der Baur.
sentences.l: “What must I do?” asked the farmer.
sentences.n: thun is the 1857 spelling of tun, to do. Baur is a spoken variant of Bauer, farmer; the tale uses both spellings within a few lines.

sentences.t: „Erstlich kauf dir ein Abcbuch, so ist eins, wo vorn ein Göckelhahn drin ist;
sentences.l: “Firstly buy yourself an ABC-book, there is one where a cockerel is in the front of it;
sentences.i: “First, buy yourself an ABC-book — there is one that has a cockerel in the front;
sentences.n: Ein Abcbuch is the primer a child learns its letters from, and the old ones opened with a picture of a cock. “so ist eins” = there is one, the kind where …. drin = darin, in it.

sentences.t: zweitens mache deinen Wagen und deine zwei Ochsen zu Geld und schaff dir damit Kleider an, und was sonst zur Doctorei gehört;
sentences.l: secondly turn your wagon and your two oxen into money and get yourself clothes with it, and what else belongs to doctoring;
sentences.i: second, turn your wagon and your two oxen into money, and with it get yourself clothes and whatever else belongs to the doctor’s trade;
sentences.n: “zu Geld machen” is to turn into cash, to sell up. “sich etwas anschaffen” is separable and reflexive — schaff dir … an, procure for yourself. Doctorei names the trade by its ending, as Bäckerei names the baker’s.

sentences.t: drittens laß dir ein Schild malen mit den Worten „ich bin der Doctor Allwissend,“ und laß das oben über deine Hausthür nageln.“
sentences.l: thirdly have a sign painted for you with the words “I am the Doctor Allwissend,” and have it nailed up over your house-door.”
sentences.i: third, have a sign painted with the words “I am Doctor Know-all,” and have it nailed up above your house door.”
sentences.n: “laß dir … malen” is lassen with an infinitive, the German way of having a thing done for you. Allwissend means all-knowing; it is kept as a name in the German, and the idiomatic line gives its sense. Hausthür is the 1857 spelling of Haustür.

sentences.t: Der Bauer that alles, wies ihm geheißen war.
sentences.l: The farmer did everything, as it had been bidden him.
sentences.i: The farmer did it all, just as he had been told.
sentences.n: wies = wie es. geheißen is the participle of heißen in its older sense of bidding, commanding: as it was bidden him. that is the 1857 spelling of tat, did.

sentences.t: Als er nun ein wenig gedoctert hatte, aber noch nicht viel, ward einem reichen großen Herrn Geld gestohlen.
sentences.l: When now he had doctored a little, but not yet much, money was stolen from a rich great lord.
sentences.i: When he had doctored a little, though not much yet, money was stolen from a rich and great lord.
sentences.n: gedoctert is coined straight from the noun — to play the doctor. ward is the old past of werden and builds the passive here, was stolen. The person robbed stands in the dative, einem Herrn: stolen from him.

sentences.t: Da ward ihm von dem Doctor Allwissend gesagt, der in dem und dem Dorfe wohnte und auch wissen müßte wo das Geld hingekommen wäre.
sentences.l: Then he was told of the Doctor Allwissend, who lived in this and that village and must also know where the money had got to.
sentences.i: Then he was told of Doctor Know-all, who lived in such and such a village and would surely know where the money had gone.
sentences.n: “in dem und dem Dorfe” = in this and that village, our “such and such.” müßte and wäre are the subjunctives of reported speech, marking this as what people said. hinkommen is to get to a place.

sentences.t: Also ließ der Herr seinen Wagen anspannen, fuhr hinaus ins Dorf und fragte bei ihm an ob er der Doctor Allwissend wäre?
sentences.l: So the lord had his wagon harnessed, drove out into the village and enquired of him whether he was the Doctor Allwissend?
sentences.i: So the lord had his carriage harnessed, drove out to the village and enquired of him whether he was Doctor Know-all.
sentences.n: anspannen is to put the horses to. “anfragen” is separable — fragte … an, made enquiry. The question mark stands although the question is only reported, as the 1857 text often does.

sentences.t: „Ja, der wär er.“
sentences.l: “Yes, that he was.”
sentences.n: This line and the two that follow are reported speech set down as though spoken: the subjunctive wär (wäre) shows they are someone’s words and not the narrator’s. der is a demonstrative, that one.

sentences.t: „So sollte er mitgehen und das gestohlene Geld wieder schaffen.“
sentences.l: “Then he should come along and get the stolen money back again.”
sentences.n: sollte again carries reported speech — the lord’s demand, given in the farmer’s hearing. “wieder schaffen” is to bring back, to procure again.

sentences.t: „O ja, aber die Grethe, seine Frau, müßte auch mit.“
sentences.l: “Oh yes, but Grethe, his wife, would have to come too.”
sentences.n: Grethe is the short form of Margarethe and stands as a name. In “müßte auch mit” the verb of motion is left out after the modal — must [go] along too — which German does freely and English cannot.

sentences.t: Der Herr war das zufrieden, und ließ sie beide in den Wagen sitzen, und sie fuhren zusammen fort.
sentences.l: The lord was that content, and let them both sit in the wagon, and they drove off together.
sentences.i: The lord was satisfied with that, and had them both sit in the carriage, and they drove off together.
sentences.n: “etwas zufrieden sein” with a bare accusative is the older construction where modern German says mit etwas zufrieden sein. fortfahren is separable, to drive away.

sentences.t: Als sie auf den adlichen Hof kamen, war der Tisch gedeckt, da sollte er erst mitessen.
sentences.l: When they came to the noble estate, the table was laid, and he was first to eat with them.
sentences.i: When they came to the nobleman’s estate, the table was laid, and he was to eat with them first.
sentences.n: adlich is the 1857 form of adelig, noble; ein Hof here is the manor with its lands. mitessen is separable, to eat along with the others.

sentences.t: „Ja, aber seine Frau, die Grethe, auch“ sagte er und setzte sich mit ihr hinter den Tisch.
sentences.l: “Yes, but his wife, Grethe, too,” he said and set himself with her behind the table.
sentences.i: “Yes, but his wife Grethe as well,” he said, and sat down with her behind the table.
sentences.n: “sich setzen” is reflexive where English simply sits down. One sits hinter den Tisch, behind the table, looking out from the seat — German counts it from the sitter’s side.

sentences.t: Wie nun der erste Bediente mit einer Schüssel schönem Essen kam, stieß der Bauer seine Frau an und sagte „Grethe, das war der erste,“ und meinte es wäre derjenige, welcher das erste Essen brächte.
sentences.l: When now the first servant came with a dish of fine food, the farmer nudged his wife and said, “Grethe, that was the first,” and meant it was the one who brought the first course.
sentences.i: Now when the first servant came in with a dish of fine food, the farmer nudged his wife and said: “Grethe, that was the first” — and he meant the one who was bringing in the first course.
sentences.n: “anstoßen” is separable, to give a nudge. This is the hinge of the tale: the farmer counts the courses, and the servants hear him counting them. Die Schüssel is the serving-dish. Essen here is the noun — the food, the course being carried in.

sentences.t: Der Bediente aber meinte er hätte damit sagen wollen „das ist der erste Dieb,“
sentences.l: The servant, however, thought he had wanted to say by it, “that is the first thief,”
sentences.i: But the servant thought he had meant to say by it, “That is the first thief,”
sentences.n: meinen is to mean, to be of an opinion. “hätte sagen wollen” is a double infinitive — had wanted to say — with the subjunctive hätte marking that this is the servant’s own construction of the words.

sentences.t: und weil ers nun wirklich war, ward ihm angst, und er sagte draußen zu seinen Kameraden „der Doctor weiß alles, wir kommen übel an: er hat gesagt ich wäre der erste.“
sentences.l: and because he really was it, fear came upon him, and he said outside to his comrades, “the doctor knows everything, we shall come off badly: he has said I was the first.”
sentences.i: and since he really was, he grew frightened, and said outside to his comrades: “The doctor knows everything, we shall come off badly — he has said that I was the first.”
sentences.n: “ihm ward angst” is impersonal: it grew fearful to him, that is, he became afraid, with the person in the dative. “übel ankommen” is to fare badly. ers = er es.

sentences.t: Der zweite wollte gar nicht herein, er mußte aber doch.
sentences.l: The second did not want to come in at all, but he had to all the same.
sentences.n: The verb of motion is left out after both modals — wollte nicht herein, mußte aber doch [herein] — a compression German allows and English has to fill in.

sentences.t: Wie er nun mit seiner Schüssel herein kam, stieß der Baur seine Frau an, „Grethe, das ist der zweite.“
sentences.l: When now he came in with his dish, the farmer nudged his wife, “Grethe, that is the second.”
sentences.n: The counting goes on, and each servant hears his own sentence in it. Baur here for Bauer again — the spelling shifts within the tale.

sentences.t: Dem Bedienten ward ebenfalls angst, und er machte daß er hinaus kam.
sentences.l: Fear came upon the servant likewise, and he made that he got out.
sentences.i: The servant grew frightened in the same way, and made shift to get out.
sentences.n: “machen, daß man …” is to see to it that one does a thing — here, to get himself out fast. The dative dem Bedienten again names the one the fear comes upon.

sentences.t: Dem dritten giengs nicht besser, der Bauer sagte wieder „Grethe, das ist der dritte.“
sentences.l: It went no better for the third; the farmer said again, “Grethe, that is the third.”
sentences.n: “es geht jemandem gut” or “schlecht” — it goes well or badly to someone — is how German says how a person fares. giengs = gieng es.

sentences.t: Der vierte mußte eine verdeckte Schüssel hereintragen, und der Herr sprach zum Doctor er sollte seine Kunst zeigen und rathen was darunter läge; es waren aber Krebse.
sentences.l: The fourth had to carry in a covered dish, and the lord spoke to the doctor that he should show his art and guess what lay underneath; but they were crayfish.
sentences.i: The fourth had to carry in a covered dish, and the lord told the doctor to show his art and guess what lay beneath it — but they were crayfish.
sentences.n: rathen is the 1857 spelling of raten, to guess or to advise. läge is the subjunctive of the reported demand. Krebse are crayfish — the same word as the farmer’s name, which is about to save him.

sentences.t: Der Bauer sah die Schüssel an, wußte nicht wie er sich helfen sollte und sprach „ach, ich armer Krebs!“
sentences.l: The farmer looked at the dish, did not know how he should help himself, and spoke, “oh, poor crab that I am!”
sentences.i: The farmer looked at the dish, did not know how to help himself, and said: “Ah, poor Krebs that I am!”
sentences.n: This is the turn the whole tale is built on: he is lamenting himself by his own name, Krebs, and the company hears him naming the crayfish under the cover. “sich helfen” is to know a way out. The pun cannot cross into English, so the literal keeps the crab and the idiomatic keeps the name.

sentences.t: Wie der Herr das hörte, rief er „da, er weiß es, nun weiß er auch wer das Geld hat.“
sentences.l: When the lord heard that, he cried, “there, he knows it, now he knows too who has the money.”
sentences.n: da here is the triumphant “there!”, pointing at what has just happened.

sentences.t: Dem Bedienten aber ward gewaltig angst und er blinzelte den Doctor an, er möchte einmal heraus kommen.
sentences.l: The servant, however, grew mightily afraid, and he blinked at the doctor that he might come out for once.
sentences.i: But the servant grew mightily afraid, and winked at the doctor to come outside a moment.
sentences.n: “anblinzeln” is separable — blinzelte … an, to wink at someone. möchte is the subjunctive of a wish passed on at second hand: would he please come out. Once more the impersonal “ihm ward angst.”

sentences.t: Wie er nun hinaus kam, gestanden sie ihm alle viere sie hätten das Geld gestohlen:
sentences.l: When now he came out, all four of them confessed to him they had stolen the money:
sentences.i: When he came out, all four of them confessed to him that they had stolen the money:
sentences.n: gestehen takes the dative of the person confessed to. hätten is the subjunctive of reported speech. “alle viere” is the old inflected form of alle vier, all four of them. gestanden here is the past of gestehen, to confess, and not of stehen, to stand, which the same form also serves.

sentences.t: sie wolltens ja gerne heraus geben und ihm eine schwere Summe dazu, wenn er sie nicht verrathen wollte: es ginge ihnen sonst an den Hals.
sentences.l: they would gladly give it out and a heavy sum to him besides, if he would not betray them: otherwise it would go to their necks.
sentences.i: they would gladly hand it over, and a heavy sum with it, if only he would not betray them — otherwise their necks were forfeit.
sentences.n: “es geht jemandem an den Hals” is the plain old phrase for a matter of life and death: theft on this scale was a hanging affair. verrathen is the 1857 spelling of verraten. wolltens = wollten es.

sentences.t: Sie führten ihn auch hin, wo das Geld versteckt lag.
sentences.l: They led him there too, where the money lay hidden.
sentences.i: They led him to the place as well, where the money lay hidden.
sentences.n: hinführen is separable — führten … hin, led him there. “versteckt lag” is the ordinary way of saying it lay hidden.

sentences.t: Damit war der Doctor zufrieden, gieng wieder hinein, setzte sich an den Tisch, und sprach „Herr, nun will ich in meinem Buch suchen wo das Geld steckt.“
sentences.l: With that the doctor was content, went in again, set himself at the table, and spoke, “my lord, now I will search in my book where the money is lodged.”
sentences.i: The doctor was content with that, went in again, sat down at the table, and said: “My lord, now I will look in my book to find where the money is.”
sentences.n: stecken is to be lodged fast, hidden away. Herr as an address is “sir, my lord.” The book is of course the ABC primer, which is the joke that follows.

sentences.t: Der fünfte Bediente aber kroch in den Ofen und wollte hören ob der Doctor noch mehr wüßte.
sentences.l: The fifth servant, however, crept into the stove and wanted to hear whether the doctor knew still more.
sentences.i: But the fifth servant crept into the stove, to hear whether the doctor knew any more.
sentences.n: Der Ofen is the great tiled stove of an old house, wide enough to hide in when it is not lit. wüßte is again the subjunctive after ob.

sentences.t: Der saß aber und schlug sein Abcbuch auf, blätterte hin und her und suchte den Göckelhahn.
sentences.l: But he sat and struck his ABC-book open, leafed hither and thither and looked for the cockerel.
sentences.i: But he sat there and opened his ABC-book, turned the leaves this way and that, and looked for the cockerel.
sentences.n: “aufschlagen” is separable and is the regular verb for opening a book. Der at the head of the sentence is a demonstrative picking up the doctor: he, that one.

sentences.t: Weil er ihn nicht gleich finden konnte, sprach er „du bist doch darin und mußt auch heraus.“
sentences.l: Because he could not find it straight away, he spoke, “you are in there after all, and must come out too.”
sentences.i: Because he could not find it at once, he said: “You are in there all the same, and out you must come.”
sentences.n: He is speaking to the cockerel in the book, and the man in the stove takes it for himself — the same trick as with the counting of the servants. The verb of motion is again left out after the modal: mußt auch heraus.

sentences.t: Da glaubte der im Ofen er wäre gemeint, sprang voller Schrecken heraus und rief „der Mann weiß alles.“
sentences.l: Then the one in the stove believed he was meant, sprang out full of terror and cried, “the man knows everything.”
sentences.i: Then the man in the stove believed that he was meant, sprang out in terror and cried: “The man knows everything!”
sentences.n: “der im Ofen” is a bare article standing for a whole phrase — the one in the stove; German does this freely where English needs a noun. wäre is the subjunctive of what he took to be the case.

sentences.t: Nun zeigte der Doctor Allwissend dem Herrn wo das Geld lag, sagte aber nicht wers gestohlen hatte, bekam von beiden Seiten viel Geld zur Belohnung, und ward ein berühmter Mann.
sentences.l: Now the Doctor Allwissend showed the lord where the money lay, but did not say who had stolen it, received much money as reward from both sides, and became a famous man.
sentences.i: Now Doctor Know-all showed the lord where the money lay, but did not say who had stolen it; he received a great deal of money from both sides as his reward, and became a famous man.
sentences.n: wers = wer es. “von beiden Seiten” — from both sides — is the sting of the ending: he is paid by the robbed man and by the thieves alike, and keeps their secret.

glossary.an: an — at, on, to; also the separable prefix of ansehen, anstoßen, anfragen, anschaffen, ankommen
glossary.drin: drin — in it, inside (colloquial contraction of darin)
glossary.eins: eins — one (neuter indefinite pronoun; so ist eins: there is one such)
glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun; also clipped onto a word: wies = wie es, ers = er es, giengs = gieng es)
glossary.essen: das Essen — food; the course brought to table (neuter noun; here not the infinitive essen)
glossary.fuhr: fahren — drove, carted (3rd sg. preterite; of driving a wagon)
glossary.fuhren: fahren — drove (3rd pl. preterite; fuhren fort: drove off)
glossary.gehört: gehören — belongs (3rd sg. present, + zu; not the past participle of hören)
glossary.gestanden: gestehen — confessed (preterite pl.; takes the dative of the person; not stehen, stood)
glossary.hof: der Hof — manor, estate; courtyard (masc. noun)
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, for him (dative of er)
glossary.ja: ja — yes; (as a particle) indeed, after all
glossary.laß: lassen — have (a thing) done; let (2nd sg. imperative; 1857 spelling of lass)
glossary.rathen: rathen — to guess (infinitive; 1857 spelling of raten; here guessing, not advising)
glossary.steckt: stecken — is lodged, is hidden (3rd sg. present, intransitive)
glossary.verrathen: verrathen — to betray, give away (infinitive; 1857 spelling of verraten)
glossary.ward: werden — became; also the passive auxiliary, was (archaic preterite of wurde; ward gestohlen: was stolen)
glossary.weiß: wissen — knows (3rd sg. present; not weiß, white)
glossary.welcher: welcher — who, which (relative pronoun, nom. masc.)
